# TCP Congestion Control

TCP congestion control prevents network collapse by regulating how much data a sender injects into the network. The sender maintains a congestion window (cwnd), which together with the receiver's advertised window bounds outstanding data. Because routers signal congestion primarily through loss, TCP infers congestion from timeouts and duplicate acknowledgments, adjusting cwnd accordingly.

## Slow Start

A connection begins in slow start with a small cwnd (historically one segment; modern stacks use up to ten). Every round-trip time (RTT) without loss doubles cwnd, producing exponential growth that rapidly discovers available capacity despite the algorithm's name. When cwnd reaches the slow start threshold (ssthresh), the sender transitions to congestion avoidance. A timeout during slow start is treated harshly: ssthresh is set to half the current cwnd, cwnd resets to one segment, and slow start restarts from the beginning.

## Congestion Avoidance

Once in congestion avoidance, growth becomes linear—cwnd increases by roughly one maximum segment size per RTT. This implements additive increase, multiplicative decrease (AIMD): steady probing for spare bandwidth, but rapid withdrawal when loss indicates congestion. Upon detecting loss, the sender halves cwnd, sets ssthresh to that value, and proceeds according to the type of loss signal observed.

## Fast Recovery

Fast recovery optimizes the response to mild congestion signaled by three duplicate ACKs rather than a timeout. Instead of collapsing back to slow start, TCP Reno halves cwnd, sets ssthresh to that value, retransmits the missing segment, and continues transmitting new data directly from congestion avoidance. This avoids wasting a full exponential ramp for a single dropped packet while the connection remains otherwise healthy.

Together these mechanisms—exponential probing, linear growth, and graceful recovery—form the loss-based control loop that has kept the Internet stable for decades. Modern variants such as NewReno, CUBIC, and BBR refine the same core principles for today's high-bandwidth, long-latency paths.

TCP congestion control prevents a sender from overwhelming the network by dynamically regulating the congestion window (cwnd), the amount of unacknowledged data in flight. Classic TCP (Tahoe/Reno lineage) achieves this through three interlocking algorithms.

Slow start begins a connection or follows severe loss with cwnd set to a small value, historically one segment, now often ten. For every acknowledgment received, cwnd doubles each round-trip time, producing exponential growth. Despite its name, slow start ramps up aggressively; it is "slow" only relative to sending an entire window immediately. Growth continues until cwnd reaches the slow start threshold (ssthresh) or loss is detected, at which point the algorithm transitions to congestion avoidance.

Congestion avoidance assumes the network is near capacity. Growth becomes linear: cwnd increases by roughly one maximum segment size per RTT (additive increase), probing cautiously for spare bandwidth. This creates the well-known sawtooth throughput pattern when combined with loss responses.

Loss detection drives the third mechanism. A retransmission timeout signals severe congestion: ssthresh is set to half the current flight window, cwnd collapses to one segment, and slow start restarts. A triple-duplicate ACK, however, signals milder congestion, typically a single lost packet. TCP Reno's fast recovery handles this by halving cwnd (multiplicative decrease), setting ssthresh accordingly, and retransmitting the missing segment immediately via fast retransmit. Crucially, the sender skips slow start entirely, continuing in congestion avoidance rather than restarting from scratch, since duplicate ACKs prove the network is still delivering data.

Together these mechanisms implement AIMD—additive increase, multiplicative decrease—a provably fair, distributed allocation strategy requiring no router support. content: Single-pin pickingSingle-pin picking exploits the tiny manufacturing tolerances in a pin tumbler lock. You insert a tension wrench into the keyway and apply slight rotational pressure, which causes the plug to bind slightly against one pin (the "binding pin") at its shear line, since pins are never machined to perfectly identical heights. Once set, that pin no longer blocks rotation, and the binding force shifts to the next most-binding pin, which you then lift and set the same way. When all pin stacks are set, the plug rotates freely and the lock opens — the core skill is keeping tension light and consistent, since too much force makes pins overset and masks the feedback that tells you which pin to work on next.

TCP congestion control regulates the rate at which data is injected into the network, preventing collapse when aggregate demand exceeds available capacity. Its modern form rests on three cooperating mechanisms: slow start, congestion avoidance, and fast recovery, all governed by a congestion window (cwnd) that caps unacknowledged bytes in flight.

Slow start governs the initial phase of every connection. The sender begins with a small cwnd—historically one or two segments, now commonly ten—and doubles it each round-trip time by incrementing cwnd by one segment per acknowledgment received. This exponential growth probes rapidly for available bandwidth but is bounded by the slow start threshold (ssthresh). When cwnd reaches ssthresh, or when packet loss signals that the network is saturated, the sender transitions to the next phase.

Congestion avoidance assumes loss indicates incipient congestion. Here, cwnd grows only linearly—one segment per round-trip time—implementing additive increase. Traditionally, a timeout or detection of loss triggered multiplicative decrease: ssthresh was set to half the current window, cwnd reset, and slow start re-entered. Modern variants such as CUBIC scale the decrease with time since the last congestion event, while delay-based algorithms like Vegas or BBR infer congestion from rising queuing delay rather than loss.

Fast recovery refines the reaction to loss. When three duplicate acknowledgments arrive—evidence that a single packet was dropped but later segments still flowed—the sender performs fast retransmit, resending the missing segment immediately rather than awaiting a timeout. It then enters fast recovery: ssthresh and cwnd are halved, and cwnd is inflated by one segment per duplicate ACK, allowing transmission to continue at a reduced rate until an ACK acknowledging the retransmission arrives, restoring the halved window.

Together these mechanisms form the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease feedback loop that keeps millions of flows stable, fair, and responsive to network conditions.

**TCP Congestion Control**

TCP congestion control regulates the rate at which a sender injects data into the network to avoid overwhelming intermediate links and routers. The canonical framework, defined in RFC 5681, comprises four intertwined algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. Each operates by maintaining a congestion window (cwnd) that bounds the volume of unacknowledged data in flight, with the effective send window being the minimum of cwnd and the receiver's advertised window.

Slow start governs the beginning of a connection or the restart after a timeout. The sender initializes cwnd to a small value—historically one segment, now commonly ten segments per RFC 6928—and doubles cwnd for every acknowledged round-trip, i.e., it increases cwnd by one segment per ACK received. This yields exponential growth, rapidly probing available capacity until cwnd reaches the slow-start threshold (ssthresh), at which point the sender transitions to congestion avoidance.

Congestion avoidance implements additive increase: cwnd grows by roughly one segment per round-trip time (approximately one segment per cwnd ACKs), producing a linear, cautious probe for additional bandwidth. This AIMD (additive increase, multiplicative decrease) behavior is the cornerstone of TCP's stability and fairness properties.

Fast retransmit triggers when the sender receives three duplicate ACKs, indicating a single segment loss without severe congestion. Rather than waiting for a retransmission timeout, the sender immediately retransmits the missing segment. Fast recovery then sets ssthresh to half the flight size and inflates cwnd to ssthresh plus three segments, temporarily inflating the window for each additional duplicate ACK to sustain transmission. Upon receipt of a new ACK, cwnd deflates to ssthresh and the sender re-enters congestion avoidance, avoiding the drastic return to slow start that a timeout would impose. Together these mechanisms balance throughput, loss recovery, and network stability.
